Выбор выхода определяется задачей, а не самим названием MLP. ## Model state: parameters, buffers, and submodules The training example passes `model.parameters()` to SGD. The optimizer receives four tensors: `fc1.weight`, `fc1.bias`, `fc2.weight`, and `fc2.bias`. It does not inspect `forward()` to find them. When `self.fc1 = nn.Linear(...)` executes, `nn.Module` registers `fc1` as a child module. `parameters()` then visits that child and finds its registered weight and bias. It does the same for `fc2`. The printed model exposes this nesting: ```text MLP( (fc1): Linear(in_features=2, out_features=3, bias=True) (fc2): Linear(in_features=3, out_features=2, bias=True) ) ``` Here `N` counts the scalar values in each tensor. | Child | Name | Shape | N | |---|---|---|---:| | `fc1` | `fc1.weight` | `[3, 2]` | 6 | | `fc1` | `fc1.bias` | `[3]` | 3 | | `fc2` | `fc2.weight` | `[2, 3]` | 6 | | `fc2` | `fc2.bias` | `[2]` | 2 | The names describe ownership; the shapes describe the stored tensors. Calling the same layer twice in `forward()` uses the same parameters twice. It creates two uses in the computation graph, not a second set of weights. Conversely, a registered child can remain unused in a particular forward pass. The module hierarchy and the graph of executed operations answer different questions. ### Registration does not depend on a gradient The following code is the complete **Parameter Registration** example from [Harvard ML Systems, ML Frameworks — Automatic parameter discovery](https://mlsysbook.ai/contents/vol1/frameworks/frameworks.html#sec-ml-frameworks-nn-module-parameter-discovery-4a91), Vijay Janapa Reddi and contributors. Code and comments are unchanged from [commit `2bd97c5`](https://github.com/harvard-edge/cs249r_book/blob/2bd97c509923dc8d7cb0b3e2f489a7282fee5fbd/book/quarto/contents/vol1/frameworks/frameworks.qmd). The source is distributed under [CC BY-NC-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-sa/4.0/); this surrounding explanation adds checks and distinguishes registration from autograd. ```python import torch import torch.nn as nn class CustomLayer(nn.Module): def __init__(self, input_size, output_size): super().__init__() self.weight = nn.Parameter( torch.randn(output_size, input_size) ) self.bias = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(output_size)) self.register_buffer("running_mean", torch.zeros(output_size)) def forward(self, x): return torch.matmul(x, self.weight.t()) + self.bias layer = CustomLayer(10, 20) # Framework discovers both parameters automatically: for name, param in layer.named_parameters(): print(f"{name}: shape {param.shape}") ``` The output lists `weight: shape torch.Size([20, 10])` and `bias: shape torch.Size([20])`: 220 parameter values. `running_mean` contains another 20 values, but is returned by `named_buffers()`, not `named_parameters()`. This example never reads or updates `running_mean` in `forward()`. The name alone does not implement a running average or normalization. Assigning an `nn.Parameter` to a module attribute triggers registration through [`Module.__setattr__`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/5c4886908584029761b579af026dcfb627c84070/torch/nn/modules/module.py#L1976). Assigning a child `nn.Module` registers that child. `super().__init__()` creates the registries before either assignment. A plain tensor assigned to a new attribute is not automatically a parameter, even with `requires_grad=True`. | State | List | Save | Move | |---|---|---|---| | Parameter | Yes | Yes | Yes | | Saved buffer | No | Yes | Yes | | Unsaved buffer | No | No | Yes | | Plain tensor | No | No | No | Here “List” means returned by `parameters()`, “Save” means included in `state_dict()`, and “Move” means handled by `.to()`. Saved buffers use `persistent=True`. An unsaved buffer uses `persistent=False`: it is omitted from the state dictionary, not cleared after each forward pass. These entries refer to ordinary non-`None` tensors and the standard module implementation. A floating-point buffer can also require gradients: registration does not disable autograd. An optimizer constructed from `model.parameters()` does not receive buffers or plain tensor attributes, regardless of their `requires_grad` flags. A parameter with `requires_grad=False` remains registered; `parameters()` does not filter it out. The distinction can be observed with a two-input, two-output instance. Set its weights to `[[2, -1], [1, 3]]` and bias to `[0.5, -0.5]`. On input `[1, 2]`, the output is `[0.5, 6.5]`. Add a separate plain tensor `plain = 2` and use `sum(output) + plain**2` as the loss. The derivative with respect to `plain` is 4, but SGD will not update it unless it is explicitly given that tensor. ```python state_probe = CustomLayer(2, 2) state_probe.plain = torch.tensor(2., requires_grad=True) state_probe.register_buffer("scratch", torch.ones(2), persistent=False) state_probe.double() assert state_probe.weight.dtype == state_probe.scratch.dtype == torch.float64 assert state_probe.plain.dtype == torch.float32 # not registered with torch.no_grad(): state_probe.weight.copy_(torch.tensor([[2., -1.], [1., 3.]])) state_probe.bias.copy_(torch.tensor([.5, -.5])) state_probe.bias.requires_grad_(False) probe_input = torch.tensor([[1., 2.]], dtype=torch.float64) probe_optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(state_probe.parameters(), lr=.1) probe_output = state_probe(probe_input) torch.testing.assert_close(probe_output, torch.tensor([[.5, 6.5]], dtype=torch.float64)) probe_loss = probe_output.sum() + state_probe.plain.square() probe_loss.backward() probe_optimizer.step() assert state_probe.plain.grad.item() == 4 and state_probe.plain.item() == 2 assert state_probe.bias.grad is None assert "bias" in dict(state_probe.named_parameters()) torch.testing.assert_close(state_probe.bias, torch.tensor([.5, -.5], dtype=torch.float64)) torch.testing.assert_close(state_probe.weight, torch.tensor([[1.9, -1.2], [.9, 2.8]], dtype=torch.float64)) assert set(state_probe.state_dict()) == {"weight", "bias", "running_mean"} ``` Both output coordinates use the input `[1, 2]`, so both weight rows receive the gradient `[1, 2]`. A step of size 0.1 subtracts `[0.1, 0.2]` from each row. The frozen bias receives no gradient in this run. The buffer remains zero because it takes no part in the computation. The plain tensor receives a gradient, but is absent from the optimizer's parameter groups. Thus a missing weight update can be a registration problem even when backward succeeds. Freezing an existing parameter during training also requires clearing any old gradient already stored in `.grad`. Setting `requires_grad=False` prevents new gradient computation; it does not erase the previous tensor, and an optimizer can still act on that tensor. In the example, the bias is frozen before its first backward pass. Freezing and gradient accumulation are developed further in the [[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/01 Основы нейронных сетей/01 Нейрон, градиент и backpropagation|backpropagation chapter]]. ### A list of layers must register its contents PyTorch's [Modules as Building Blocks](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/notes/modules.html#modules-as-building-blocks) describes the recursive rule: > For any given module, its parameters consist of its direct parameters as well > as the parameters of all submodules. A Python list does not register the modules stored inside it. `nn.ModuleList` does. It stores layers for use by your `forward()`; it does not define a forward computation of its own. `nn.Sequential` additionally defines a computation that passes each layer's output into the next layer. The following comparison uses the same two `CustomLayer` objects in both containers, so differences cannot be attributed to random initialization. ```python class LayerStack(nn.Module): def __init__(self, blocks, register): super().__init__() self.blocks = nn.ModuleList(blocks) if register else list(blocks) def forward(self, x): for block in self.blocks: x = torch.relu(block(x)) return x stack_blocks = [CustomLayer(2, 2), CustomLayer(2, 2)] plain_stack = LayerStack(stack_blocks, register=False) registered_stack = LayerStack(stack_blocks, register=True) stack_input = torch.tensor([[1., 2.]]) torch.testing.assert_close(plain_stack(stack_input), registered_stack(stack_input)) assert list(plain_stack.parameters()) == [] assert plain_stack.state_dict() == {} assert sum(p.numel() for p in registered_stack.parameters()) == 12 assert set(registered_stack.state_dict()) == { "blocks.0.weight", "blocks.0.bias", "blocks.0.running_mean", "blocks.1.weight", "blocks.1.bias", "blocks.1.running_mean", } ``` Both forward calls work: Python can call a layer from an ordinary list, and autograd can differentiate its tensor operations. Only `registered_stack` exposes those layers to recursive module operations. For `plain_stack`, an optimizer built from `parameters()` would receive an empty list. A model with other correctly registered layers could instead train only that subset, leaving the omitted layers unchanged without an empty-list error. The registered stack has 12 parameter values: two copies of a 2×2 weight and a length-2 bias. Its six state entries also include two length-2 buffers. Parameter count and number of state entries count different objects. The test deliberately shares the two layer objects between containers; updating them through one container also affects the other. ### Saving values and rebuilding the computation `state_dict()` returns named parameters and persistent buffers, including those of registered children. The dotted key `blocks.0.weight` identifies the weight of the first layer in `blocks`. It does not encode the ReLU in `forward()`, the Python loop, or a constructor that can rebuild `LayerStack`. Construct the destination model first, then load its tensor values. This example serializes the modified `state_probe` in memory rather than creating an extra file: ```python import io checkpoint_bytes = io.BytesIO() torch.save(state_probe.state_dict(), checkpoint_bytes) checkpoint_bytes.seek(0) loaded_state = torch.load(checkpoint_bytes, weights_only=True) restored_layer = CustomLayer(2, 2).double() restored_layer.load_state_dict(loaded_state) torch.testing.assert_close(restored_layer(probe_input), state_probe(probe_input)) torch.testing.assert_close(restored_layer(probe_input), torch.tensor([[0., 6.]], dtype=torch.float64)) assert not hasattr(restored_layer, "plain") assert not hasattr(restored_layer, "scratch") assert restored_layer.bias.requires_grad # constructor default, not saved freeze state ``` `load_state_dict()` fills a compatible module that already exists. It does not reconstruct its hierarchy from key names. A shape mismatch remains an error even with `strict=False`; that option permits missing or unexpected keys, not arbitrary conversion between architectures. The frozen bias's *value* was restored, but its `requires_grad` flag came from the destination object. The plain attribute and non-persistent buffer were not saved. The returned state dictionary also holds references to the module's current state. Keeping `best_state = model.state_dict()` in memory does not freeze a historical copy; subsequent in-place updates can change the referenced values. Use a deep copy when retaining a best model in memory. A resumable training checkpoint needs optimizer state and other run state as well; the [[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/01 Основы нейронных сетей/02 Оптимизация и стабильность обучения|optimization chapter]] contains a complete save/resume example. ### Evaluation mode and gradient recording Calling `.eval()` recursively sets the registered modules' `training` flags to `False`. Layers that use this flag can then select evaluation behavior; the `Linear` layers and functional ReLU in our MLP do not change their formula. Dropout and BatchNorm will use it in later chapters. `.eval()` does not disable gradient recording or freeze parameters. ```python mode_probe = MLP(2, 3, 2).double().eval() mode_input = torch.ones(1, 2, dtype=torch.float64) assert all(not module.training for module in mode_probe.modules()) assert mode_probe(mode_input).requires_grad with torch.no_grad(): assert not mode_probe(mode_input).requires_grad assert all(p.requires_grad for p in mode_probe.parameters()) ``` Use `model(x)` rather than calling `model.forward(x)` directly: the module call also runs registered hooks. The full API contracts and original English examples are in PyTorch's [Modules](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/notes/modules.html) and [Module](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/generated/torch.nn.Module.html) documentation. The PyTorch excerpt above is reproduced under its [BSD-style license](/licenses/pytorch-v2.14.1-LICENSE.txt). ## Observing a layer: forward and backward hooks A forward hook receives a layer's inputs and computed output. A full backward hook receives derivatives with respect to its inputs and outputs. The weights and bias of `Linear` are attributes of the module, not positional inputs to its `forward(x)`: their gradients are not entries in `grad_input`. The complete original example below is from Vijay Janapa Reddi and Harvard ML Systems contributors, [ML Frameworks, Module Hooks](https://github.com/harvard-edge/cs249r_book/blob/2bd97c509923dc8d7cb0b3e2f489a7282fee5fbd/book/quarto/contents/vol1/frameworks/frameworks.qmd#L3871), CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. Code and English comments are unchanged. ```python import torch import torch.nn as nn model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(10, 20), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(20, 5)) # Forward hook to inspect activations def forward_hook(module, input, output): print( f"Layer: {module.__class__.__name__}, " f"Output shape: {output.shape}, " f"mean={output.mean():.3f}, " f"std={output.std():.3f}" ) # Backward hook to inspect gradients def backward_hook(module, grad_input, grad_output): print(f"Gradient norm: {grad_output[0].norm():.3f}") # Register hooks on specific layer handle_fwd = model[0].register_forward_hook(forward_hook) handle_bwd = model[0].register_full_backward_hook(backward_hook) # Execute forward and backward pass x = torch.randn(32, 10) y = model(x) loss = y.sum() loss.backward() # Remove hooks when done handle_fwd.remove() handle_bwd.remove() ``` Both hooks are attached to the first `Linear`. Its output has shape `[32,20]`; the final model output has shape `[32,5]`. The sum seeds the derivative of those final outputs with ones. Before reaching the observed layer, that derivative passes through the second linear map and the ReLU mask. Thus the printed norm describes a `[32,20]` derivative, not an all-ones array or the first layer's weight gradient. The mean and standard deviation likewise summarize all entries of that layer's output, mixing batch and feature axes. Those two statistics cannot establish how each individual feature behaves. ### One layer, three different derivatives Use the same two-input, two-output weights as the state example above, before its SGD update. PyTorch stores the weight rows as `[[2,-1],[1,3]]`, with bias `[0.5,-0.5]`. On input `[1,2]` the output is `[0.5,6.5]`. Choose the scalar loss $L=z_1+2z_2=13.5$. The output derivative is `[1,2]`: increasing the second output by a small amount changes this loss twice as much as increasing the first. The input derivatives combine both output paths. For the first input, $1\cdot2+2\cdot1=4$; for the second, $1\cdot(-1)+2\cdot3=5$. Each weight derivative instead multiplies its output's incoming derivative by the corresponding input value. The vector norms below are Euclidean; the matrix norm is Frobenius. | Quantity | Values | Norm | |---|---|---| | `grad_output[0]` | `[1,2]` | $\sqrt5$ | | `grad_input[0]` | `[4,5]` | $\sqrt{41}$ | | `weight.grad` | `[1,2]`
`[2,4]` | $5$ | The bias derivative is `[1,2]`. Its numerical equality with the output derivative comes from adding one bias vector to this one example; with a batch, the bias gradient sums the output derivatives over examples. The [[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/01 Основы нейронных сетей/01 Нейрон, градиент и backpropagation|backpropagation chapter]] derives these matrix rules. The following observation function keeps detached copies, so the records do not retain the training graph. Neither callback returns a replacement tensor. Handles are removed even if the computation raises an exception. ```python def inspect_linear(input_requires_grad, parameters_require_grad, evaluation=False): observed_layer = nn.Linear(2, 2).double().train(not evaluation) with torch.no_grad(): observed_layer.weight.copy_(torch.tensor([[2., -1.], [1., 3.]])) observed_layer.bias.copy_(torch.tensor([.5, -.5])) observed_layer.requires_grad_(parameters_require_grad) records = [] def capture_forward(module, args, output): records.append({"stage": "forward", "output": output.detach().clone()}) def capture_backward(module, grad_input, grad_output): records.append({ "stage": "backward", "input_gradient": None if grad_input[0] is None else grad_input[0].detach().clone(), "output_gradient": grad_output[0].detach().clone(), }) forward_handle = observed_layer.register_forward_hook(capture_forward) backward_handle = observed_layer.register_full_backward_hook(capture_backward) observed_input = torch.tensor([[1., 2.]], dtype=torch.float64, requires_grad=input_requires_grad) try: observed_output = observed_layer(observed_input) coefficients = observed_output.new_tensor([[1., 2.]]) observed_loss = (observed_output * coefficients).sum() if observed_loss.requires_grad: observed_loss.backward() finally: forward_handle.remove() backward_handle.remove() count = len(records) with torch.no_grad(): observed_layer(observed_input) assert len(records) == count # removed hooks no longer observe the layer return observed_layer, observed_input, records, observed_loss.detach() observed_layer, observed_input, observed_records, observed_loss = inspect_linear(True, True) forward_record, backward_record = observed_records torch.testing.assert_close(forward_record["output"], observed_input.new_tensor([[.5, 6.5]])) torch.testing.assert_close(observed_loss, observed_input.new_tensor(13.5)) torch.testing.assert_close(backward_record["output_gradient"], observed_input.new_tensor([[1., 2.]])) torch.testing.assert_close(backward_record["input_gradient"], observed_input.new_tensor([[4., 5.]])) torch.testing.assert_close(observed_layer.weight.grad, observed_input.new_tensor([[1., 2.], [2., 4.]])) torch.testing.assert_close(observed_layer.bias.grad, observed_input.new_tensor([1., 2.])) torch.testing.assert_close(observed_input.grad, backward_record["input_gradient"]) ``` ### When the backward hook fires In the original Harvard example the input does not require gradients, but the layer's parameters do. Its output therefore participates in autograd, and the full backward hook observes the output derivative. It has no input derivative to report. Freezing parameters while requesting an input derivative produces the opposite parameter-storage result: the hook still runs and the input receives a derivative, but `weight.grad` remains `None`. PyTorch 2.14 emits a warning for output-side firing when no inputs require gradients. This follows the documented second firing rule; it does not mean that the parameter gradient is missing. | Input flag | Params flag | Backward record | Weight `.grad` | |---|---|---|---| | Yes | Yes | Input `[4,5]`, output `[1,2]` | Present | | No | Yes | Input `None`, output `[1,2]` | Present | | Yes | No | Input `[4,5]`, output `[1,2]` | `None` | | No | No | No backward record | `None` | ```python for input_grad in (False, True): for parameter_grad in (False, True): case_layer, case_input, case_records, _ = inspect_linear(input_grad, parameter_grad) assert len(case_records) == 1 + int(input_grad or parameter_grad) assert (case_layer.weight.grad is not None) == parameter_grad assert (case_input.grad is not None) == input_grad if input_grad or parameter_grad: observed = case_records[1] assert (observed["input_gradient"] is not None) == input_grad torch.testing.assert_close(observed["output_gradient"], case_input.new_tensor([[1., 2.]])) # eval changes layer behavior, not whether autograd records these operations. _, _, eval_records, _ = inspect_linear(True, True, evaluation=True) assert [record["stage"] for record in eval_records] == ["forward", "backward"] with torch.no_grad(): _, _, no_grad_records, _ = inspect_linear(True, True) assert [record["stage"] for record in no_grad_records] == ["forward"] ``` For this one-input `Linear`, `grad_input` and `grad_output` are one-element tuples. More general module hooks receive derivatives for positional inputs; keyword arguments are not included in `grad_input`. PyTorch's [full-backward-hook contract](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/generated/torch.nn.Module.html#torch.nn.Module.register_full_backward_hook) specifies the firing rules and the restriction on in-place modification of inputs and outputs. Full backward hooks introduce views around those tensors. Calling `forward` directly bypasses the module-call machinery that installs the hooks. The numerical layer operation still runs and autograd can still differentiate it: ```python bypass_layer = nn.Linear(2, 2).double() bypass_input = torch.ones(1, 2, dtype=torch.float64, requires_grad=True) bypass_records = [] bypass_fwd = bypass_layer.register_forward_hook(lambda *args: bypass_records.append("forward")) bypass_bwd = bypass_layer.register_full_backward_hook(lambda *args: bypass_records.append("backward")) try: bypass_layer.forward(bypass_input).sum().backward() assert bypass_records == [] and bypass_input.grad is not None bypass_layer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True) bypass_input.grad = None bypass_layer(bypass_input).sum().backward() assert bypass_records == ["forward", "backward"] finally: bypass_fwd.remove() bypass_bwd.remove() ``` Hooks can also change outputs or replace input derivatives when they return replacement values. The callbacks here return `None` and only record values. Recording every activation, computing reductions and printing scalars adds work and can change memory use or timing. These CPU examples establish what is observed; they are not a low-overhead profiler or a compiler/GPU benchmark.

A parameter with `requires_grad=False` remains registered; `parameters()` does not filter it out. The distinction can be observed with a two-input, two-output instance. Set its weights to `[[2, -1], [1, 3]]` and bias to `[0.5, -0.5]`. On input `[1, 2]`, the output is `[0.5, 6.5]`. Add a separate plain tensor `plain = 2` and use `sum(output) + plain**2` as the loss. The derivative with respect to `plain` is 4, but SGD will not update it unless it is explicitly given that tensor. ```python state_probe = CustomLayer(2, 2) state_probe.plain = torch.tensor(2., requires_grad=True) state_probe.register_buffer("scratch", torch.ones(2), persistent=False) state_probe.double() assert state_probe.weight.dtype == state_probe.scratch.dtype == torch.float64 assert state_probe.plain.dtype == torch.float32 # not registered with torch.no_grad(): state_probe.weight.copy_(torch.tensor([[2., -1.], [1., 3.]])) state_probe.bias.copy_(torch.tensor([.5, -.5])) state_probe.bias.requires_grad_(False) probe_input = torch.tensor([[1., 2.]], dtype=torch.float64) probe_optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(state_probe.parameters(), lr=.1) probe_output = state_probe(probe_input) torch.testing.assert_close(probe_output, torch.tensor([[.5, 6.5]], dtype=torch.float64)) probe_loss = probe_output.sum() + state_probe.plain.square() probe_loss.backward() probe_optimizer.step() assert state_probe.plain.grad.item() == 4 and state_probe.plain.item() == 2 assert state_probe.bias.grad is None assert "bias" in dict(state_probe.named_parameters()) torch.testing.assert_close(state_probe.bias, torch.tensor([.5, -.5], dtype=torch.float64)) torch.testing.assert_close(state_probe.weight, torch.tensor([[1.9, -1.2], [.9, 2.8]], dtype=torch.float64)) assert set(state_probe.state_dict()) == {"weight", "bias", "running_mean"} ``` Both output coordinates use the input `[1, 2]`, so both weight rows receive the gradient `[1, 2]`. A step of size 0.1 subtracts `[0.1, 0.2]` from each row. The frozen bias receives no gradient in this run. The buffer remains zero because it takes no part in the computation. The plain tensor receives a gradient, but is absent from the optimizer's parameter groups. Thus a missing weight update can be a registration problem even when backward succeeds. Freezing an existing parameter during training also requires clearing any old gradient already stored in `.grad`. Setting `requires_grad=False` prevents new gradient computation; it does not erase the previous tensor, and an optimizer can still act on that tensor. In the example, the bias is frozen before its first backward pass. Freezing and gradient accumulation are developed further in the [[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/01 Основы нейронных сетей/01 Нейрон, градиент и backpropagation|backpropagation chapter]]. #### A list of layers must register its contents PyTorch's [Modules as Building Blocks](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/notes/modules.html#modules-as-building-blocks) describes the recursive rule: > For any given module, its parameters consist of its direct parameters as well > as the parameters of all submodules. A Python list does not register the modules stored inside it. `nn.ModuleList` does. It stores layers for use by your `forward()`; it does not define a forward computation of its own. `nn.Sequential` additionally defines a computation that passes each layer's output into the next layer. The following comparison uses the same two `CustomLayer` objects in both containers, so differences cannot be attributed to random initialization. ```python class LayerStack(nn.Module): def __init__(self, blocks, register): super().__init__() self.blocks = nn.ModuleList(blocks) if register else list(blocks) def forward(self, x): for block in self.blocks: x = torch.relu(block(x)) return x stack_blocks = [CustomLayer(2, 2), CustomLayer(2, 2)] plain_stack = LayerStack(stack_blocks, register=False) registered_stack = LayerStack(stack_blocks, register=True) stack_input = torch.tensor([[1., 2.]]) torch.testing.assert_close(plain_stack(stack_input), registered_stack(stack_input)) assert list(plain_stack.parameters()) == [] assert plain_stack.state_dict() == {} assert sum(p.numel() for p in registered_stack.parameters()) == 12 assert set(registered_stack.state_dict()) == { "blocks.0.weight", "blocks.0.bias", "blocks.0.running_mean", "blocks.1.weight", "blocks.1.bias", "blocks.1.running_mean", } ``` Both forward calls work: Python can call a layer from an ordinary list, and autograd can differentiate its tensor operations. Only `registered_stack` exposes those layers to recursive module operations. For `plain_stack`, an optimizer built from `parameters()` would receive an empty list. A model with other correctly registered layers could instead train only that subset, leaving the omitted layers unchanged without an empty-list error. The registered stack has 12 parameter values: two copies of a 2×2 weight and a length-2 bias. Its six state entries also include two length-2 buffers. Parameter count and number of state entries count different objects. The test deliberately shares the two layer objects between containers; updating them through one container also affects the other. #### Saving values and rebuilding the computation `state_dict()` returns named parameters and persistent buffers, including those of registered children. The dotted key `blocks.0.weight` identifies the weight of the first layer in `blocks`. It does not encode the ReLU in `forward()`, the Python loop, or a constructor that can rebuild `LayerStack`. Construct the destination model first, then load its tensor values. This example serializes the modified `state_probe` in memory rather than creating an extra file: ```python import io checkpoint_bytes = io.BytesIO() torch.save(state_probe.state_dict(), checkpoint_bytes) checkpoint_bytes.seek(0) loaded_state = torch.load(checkpoint_bytes, weights_only=True) restored_layer = CustomLayer(2, 2).double() restored_layer.load_state_dict(loaded_state) torch.testing.assert_close(restored_layer(probe_input), state_probe(probe_input)) torch.testing.assert_close(restored_layer(probe_input), torch.tensor([[0., 6.]], dtype=torch.float64)) assert not hasattr(restored_layer, "plain") assert not hasattr(restored_layer, "scratch") assert restored_layer.bias.requires_grad # constructor default, not saved freeze state ``` `load_state_dict()` fills a compatible module that already exists. It does not reconstruct its hierarchy from key names. A shape mismatch remains an error even with `strict=False`; that option permits missing or unexpected keys, not arbitrary conversion between architectures. The frozen bias's *value* was restored, but its `requires_grad` flag came from the destination object. The plain attribute and non-persistent buffer were not saved. The returned state dictionary also holds references to the module's current state. Keeping `best_state = model.state_dict()` in memory does not freeze a historical copy; subsequent in-place updates can change the referenced values. Use a deep copy when retaining a best model in memory. A resumable training checkpoint needs optimizer state and other run state as well; the [[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/01 Основы нейронных сетей/02 Оптимизация и стабильность обучения|optimization chapter]] contains a complete save/resume example. #### Evaluation mode and gradient recording Calling `.eval()` recursively sets the registered modules' `training` flags to `False`. Layers that use this flag can then select evaluation behavior; the `Linear` layers and functional ReLU in our MLP do not change their formula. Dropout and BatchNorm will use it in later chapters. `.eval()` does not disable gradient recording or freeze parameters. ```python mode_probe = MLP(2, 3, 2).double().eval() mode_input = torch.ones(1, 2, dtype=torch.float64) assert all(not module.training for module in mode_probe.modules()) assert mode_probe(mode_input).requires_grad with torch.no_grad(): assert not mode_probe(mode_input).requires_grad assert all(p.requires_grad for p in mode_probe.parameters()) ``` Use `model(x)` rather than calling `model.forward(x)` directly: the module call also runs registered hooks. The full API contracts and original English examples are in PyTorch's [Modules](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/notes/modules.html) and [Module](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/generated/torch.nn.Module.html) documentation. The PyTorch excerpt above is reproduced under its [BSD-style license](/licenses/pytorch-v2.14.1-LICENSE.txt). ### Observing a layer: forward and backward hooks A forward hook receives a layer's inputs and computed output. A full backward hook receives derivatives with respect to its inputs and outputs. The weights and bias of `Linear` are attributes of the module, not positional inputs to its `forward(x)`: their gradients are not entries in `grad_input`. The complete original example below is from Vijay Janapa Reddi and Harvard ML Systems contributors, [ML Frameworks, Module Hooks](https://github.com/harvard-edge/cs249r_book/blob/2bd97c509923dc8d7cb0b3e2f489a7282fee5fbd/book/quarto/contents/vol1/frameworks/frameworks.qmd#L3871), CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. Code and English comments are unchanged. ```python import torch import torch.nn as nn model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(10, 20), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(20, 5)) # Forward hook to inspect activations def forward_hook(module, input, output): print( f"Layer: {module.__class__.__name__}, " f"Output shape: {output.shape}, " f"mean={output.mean():.3f}, " f"std={output.std():.3f}" ) # Backward hook to inspect gradients def backward_hook(module, grad_input, grad_output): print(f"Gradient norm: {grad_output[0].norm():.3f}") # Register hooks on specific layer handle_fwd = model[0].register_forward_hook(forward_hook) handle_bwd = model[0].register_full_backward_hook(backward_hook) # Execute forward and backward pass x = torch.randn(32, 10) y = model(x) loss = y.sum() loss.backward() # Remove hooks when done handle_fwd.remove() handle_bwd.remove() ``` Both hooks are attached to the first `Linear`. Its output has shape `[32,20]`; the final model output has shape `[32,5]`. The sum seeds the derivative of those final outputs with ones. Before reaching the observed layer, that derivative passes through the second linear map and the ReLU mask. Thus the printed norm describes a `[32,20]` derivative, not an all-ones array or the first layer's weight gradient. The mean and standard deviation likewise summarize all entries of that layer's output, mixing batch and feature axes. Those two statistics cannot establish how each individual feature behaves. #### One layer, three different derivatives Use the same two-input, two-output weights as the state example above, before its SGD update. PyTorch stores the weight rows as `[[2,-1],[1,3]]`, with bias `[0.5,-0.5]`. On input `[1,2]` the output is `[0.5,6.5]`. Choose the scalar loss $L=z_1+2z_2=13.5$. The output derivative is `[1,2]`: increasing the second output by a small amount changes this loss twice as much as increasing the first. The input derivatives combine both output paths. For the first input, $1\cdot2+2\cdot1=4$; for the second, $1\cdot(-1)+2\cdot3=5$. Each weight derivative instead multiplies its output's incoming derivative by the corresponding input value. The vector norms below are Euclidean; the matrix norm is Frobenius. | Quantity | Values | Norm | |---|---|---| | `grad_output[0]` | `[1,2]` | $\sqrt5$ | | `grad_input[0]` | `[4,5]` | $\sqrt{41}$ | | `weight.grad` | `[1,2]`
`[2,4]` | $5$ | The bias derivative is `[1,2]`. Its numerical equality with the output derivative comes from adding one bias vector to this one example; with a batch, the bias gradient sums the output derivatives over examples. The [[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/01 Основы нейронных сетей/01 Нейрон, градиент и backpropagation|backpropagation chapter]] derives these matrix rules. The following observation function keeps detached copies, so the records do not retain the training graph. Neither callback returns a replacement tensor. Handles are removed even if the computation raises an exception. ```python def inspect_linear(input_requires_grad, parameters_require_grad, evaluation=False): observed_layer = nn.Linear(2, 2).double().train(not evaluation) with torch.no_grad(): observed_layer.weight.copy_(torch.tensor([[2., -1.], [1., 3.]])) observed_layer.bias.copy_(torch.tensor([.5, -.5])) observed_layer.requires_grad_(parameters_require_grad) records = [] def capture_forward(module, args, output): records.append({"stage": "forward", "output": output.detach().clone()}) def capture_backward(module, grad_input, grad_output): records.append({ "stage": "backward", "input_gradient": None if grad_input[0] is None else grad_input[0].detach().clone(), "output_gradient": grad_output[0].detach().clone(), }) forward_handle = observed_layer.register_forward_hook(capture_forward) backward_handle = observed_layer.register_full_backward_hook(capture_backward) observed_input = torch.tensor([[1., 2.]], dtype=torch.float64, requires_grad=input_requires_grad) try: observed_output = observed_layer(observed_input) coefficients = observed_output.new_tensor([[1., 2.]]) observed_loss = (observed_output * coefficients).sum() if observed_loss.requires_grad: observed_loss.backward() finally: forward_handle.remove() backward_handle.remove() count = len(records) with torch.no_grad(): observed_layer(observed_input) assert len(records) == count # removed hooks no longer observe the layer return observed_layer, observed_input, records, observed_loss.detach() observed_layer, observed_input, observed_records, observed_loss = inspect_linear(True, True) forward_record, backward_record = observed_records torch.testing.assert_close(forward_record["output"], observed_input.new_tensor([[.5, 6.5]])) torch.testing.assert_close(observed_loss, observed_input.new_tensor(13.5)) torch.testing.assert_close(backward_record["output_gradient"], observed_input.new_tensor([[1., 2.]])) torch.testing.assert_close(backward_record["input_gradient"], observed_input.new_tensor([[4., 5.]])) torch.testing.assert_close(observed_layer.weight.grad, observed_input.new_tensor([[1., 2.], [2., 4.]])) torch.testing.assert_close(observed_layer.bias.grad, observed_input.new_tensor([1., 2.])) torch.testing.assert_close(observed_input.grad, backward_record["input_gradient"]) ``` #### When the backward hook fires In the original Harvard example the input does not require gradients, but the layer's parameters do. Its output therefore participates in autograd, and the full backward hook observes the output derivative. It has no input derivative to report. Freezing parameters while requesting an input derivative produces the opposite parameter-storage result: the hook still runs and the input receives a derivative, but `weight.grad` remains `None`. PyTorch 2.14 emits a warning for output-side firing when no inputs require gradients. This follows the documented second firing rule; it does not mean that the parameter gradient is missing. | Input flag | Params flag | Backward record | Weight `.grad` | |---|---|---|---| | Yes | Yes | Input `[4,5]`, output `[1,2]` | Present | | No | Yes | Input `None`, output `[1,2]` | Present | | Yes | No | Input `[4,5]`, output `[1,2]` | `None` | | No | No | No backward record | `None` | ```python for input_grad in (False, True): for parameter_grad in (False, True): case_layer, case_input, case_records, _ = inspect_linear(input_grad, parameter_grad) assert len(case_records) == 1 + int(input_grad or parameter_grad) assert (case_layer.weight.grad is not None) == parameter_grad assert (case_input.grad is not None) == input_grad if input_grad or parameter_grad: observed = case_records[1] assert (observed["input_gradient"] is not None) == input_grad torch.testing.assert_close(observed["output_gradient"], case_input.new_tensor([[1., 2.]])) # eval changes layer behavior, not whether autograd records these operations. _, _, eval_records, _ = inspect_linear(True, True, evaluation=True) assert [record["stage"] for record in eval_records] == ["forward", "backward"] with torch.no_grad(): _, _, no_grad_records, _ = inspect_linear(True, True) assert [record["stage"] for record in no_grad_records] == ["forward"] ``` For this one-input `Linear`, `grad_input` and `grad_output` are one-element tuples. More general module hooks receive derivatives for positional inputs; keyword arguments are not included in `grad_input`. PyTorch's [full-backward-hook contract](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/generated/torch.nn.Module.html#torch.nn.Module.register_full_backward_hook) specifies the firing rules and the restriction on in-place modification of inputs and outputs. Full backward hooks introduce views around those tensors. Calling `forward` directly bypasses the module-call machinery that installs the hooks. The numerical layer operation still runs and autograd can still differentiate it: ```python bypass_layer = nn.Linear(2, 2).double() bypass_input = torch.ones(1, 2, dtype=torch.float64, requires_grad=True) bypass_records = [] bypass_fwd = bypass_layer.register_forward_hook(lambda *args: bypass_records.append("forward")) bypass_bwd = bypass_layer.register_full_backward_hook(lambda *args: bypass_records.append("backward")) try: bypass_layer.forward(bypass_input).sum().backward() assert bypass_records == [] and bypass_input.grad is not None bypass_layer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True) bypass_input.grad = None bypass_layer(bypass_input).sum().backward() assert bypass_records == ["forward", "backward"] finally: bypass_fwd.remove() bypass_bwd.remove() ``` Hooks can also change outputs or replace input derivatives when they return replacement values. The callbacks here return `None` and only record values. Recording every activation, computing reductions and printing scalars adds work and can change memory use or timing. These CPU examples establish what is observed; they are not a low-overhead profiler or a compiler/GPU benchmark.

fullyRead.scope: Entire Hidden Layers section: limitations of linear maps, incorporating hidden layers, affine collapse, nonlinear composition and universal approximators. Later activation functions not counted in this source read.
Entire Positionwise Feed-Forward Networks section, all four implementations and same-inputs example. The remainder of Transformer source not freshly read.

Quick intro, Modeling one neuron through classifier, architecture section through summary/references. Activation-function subsection belongs to the next owner. Three original figures and pinned license freshly byte-compared.

Full nn.Module Abstraction section from 3689 through 3866 and complete Module Hooks listing 3871-3910. Automatic registration, mode-dependent behavior, composition/serialization/freezing compared with current English appendix; no claim of whole Harvard chapter read.
All ten cells' source and text outputs. Saved output at cell8 is byte-identical to retained two-moons PNG; no training rerun or fresh performance claim.

mechanisms.example: XOR impossible linear inequalities, explicit two-unit construction, X/Z/H/logits/softmax/CE and one SGD update, width/depth/parameter count and tokenwise shared FFN all retained. Moved implementation state/hooks after this complete chain.

Full unchanged Harvard CustomLayer code, plain tensor with gradient but absent optimizer, persistent/nonpersistent buffer distinction, ModuleList versus plain list, shared instances, strict and shallow state_dict, eval versus no_grad retained.
mechanisms.limits: Do not copy the source's metaclass attribution: Module.__setattr__ performs registration. Registration is independent of requires_grad; buffers can require gradients, frozen parameters remain registered. state_dict fills an existing model and does not reconstruct its architecture.

mechanisms.example: All four actual programs retained. Separate [1,2] output, [4,5] input and [[1,2],[2,4]] parameter derivatives; firing matrix, direct-forward bypass, detached copies and cleanup retained.
mechanisms.limits: Printed gradient norm is grad_output, not weight.grad or an all-ones derivative. CPU diagnostic examples are not a low-overhead profiler or GPU benchmark.

mechanisms.example: Three complete CS231n network/width/regularization images and one original micrograd two-moons output retained; meaningful alt text added.
mechanisms.limits: Width panels do not compare depth or prove held-out quality. Regularization smoothness is an observed run, not a theorem. Micrograd h=.25 plotting raster is not exact network geometry.

exclusions: Do not import CS231n's unconditional recommendation to always choose the largest network, or its old absolute statements about useful layer depth.
Do not claim the repository MIT license covers unrelated lecture-slide PDFs or third-party figures.
Do not import D2L's unqualified any-function statement as a global uniform theorem; the chapter keeps continuous functions on compact domains with suitable nonlinearities.
Nielsen, TinyTorch and Machine Learning Visualized remain further-reading links, not newly integrated entire courses.
